# Core Session Specification

Implemented user-facing contract for the **MiniPty** core session API.

## Entry Point

`Pty.Start(PtyStartInfo)` spawns a child process attached to a new pseudo-terminal and returns a `PtySession`. It does **not** wait for the child to exit.

`PtyStartInfo` supplies:

| Member | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `FileName` | Executable path or name. Required. A name without a root is searched for on the child's `PATH`: on Unix by the child, on Windows by MiniPty when `Environment` sets or removes `PATH` and otherwise by `CreateProcess`. See [Program lookup](#program-lookup-windows). On Windows a `.bat` or `.cmd` file runs through `cmd.exe` with its arguments escaped for it. See [Batch files](#batch-files-windows). A program that cannot be started, or a `WorkingDirectory` that cannot be entered, fails `Pty.Start` with `Win32Exception` on every platform; on Unix its `NativeErrorCode` is the `errno` the child reported ([Start failure report](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#start-failure-report)). |
| `Arguments` | Arguments after the executable. Default is empty. Each reaches a program as one argument, quoted with the MSVCRT rules. For a batch file each is escaped for `cmd.exe` and becomes one parameter of the script. See [Batch files](#batch-files-windows). |
| `CommandLine` | Optional pre-escaped Windows argument command line. Mutually exclusive with `Arguments`, and unsupported on Unix. Passed without any escaping, also to a batch file. |
| `WorkingDirectory` | Optional child working directory. Null inherits the parent working directory. |
| `Size` | Initial terminal columns x rows. Default is 80x24. Each dimension is clamped to the platform limit at spawn and on `Resize`: 1–32767 on Windows (ConPTY's signed 16-bit `COORD`), 1–65535 on Unix (`winsize`). `PtySession.Size` reports the value applied. |
| `Environment` | Optional child environment overlay. Null inherits the parent environment. Non-null entries override or remove inherited variables. On Windows, setting or removing `PATH` also makes MiniPty look `FileName` up on the child's `PATH`. See [Program lookup](#program-lookup-windows). |
| `TerminalName` | Optional Unix terminal name for `TERM`. Null or empty uses default behavior. Currently ignored on Windows. |
| `InheritCursor` | Default `false`. On Windows, start the child at the frontend's cursor instead of on a cleared screen (node-pty `conptyInheritCursor`); the frontend must answer ConPTY's cursor position query. Ignored on Unix, which already starts at the frontend's cursor. See [Inherited cursor](#inherited-cursor). |
| `KillProcessTree` | Default `false`. On Windows, run the child in a kill-on-close job, so `Dispose`, `Kill`, and the end of the host process, including a crash, end every process the child started. Ignored on Unix. See [Process tree](#process-tree). |
| `ConPty` | Default `null`: the ConPTY Windows ships. A `ConPtyLibrary` the application loaded runs the session on the out-of-band ConPTY (`conpty.dll` plus `OpenConsole.exe`) it supplies. Windows only. See [Out-of-band ConPTY](#out-of-band-conpty). |

`FileName`, each argument, `WorkingDirectory`, and `CommandLine` cannot contain a NUL. `Pty.Start` throws `ArgumentException` on every platform before anything is created, as it already did for the environment. The operating system reads each value as a NUL-terminated string, so a NUL would end it early: what started would not be what the string names, and a caller that checked the string would have checked something else ([Untrusted program names](#untrusted-program-names-and-paths)).

## Batch Files (Windows)

`CreateProcess` runs a batch file by starting `cmd.exe` on the command line it is given, and `cmd.exe` does not parse that line by the MSVCRT rules that programs built on the C runtime follow. An argument quoted by those rules could therefore close `cmd.exe`'s quoting and run a command: `x" & echo INJECTED & "` printed `INJECTED` from a `.cmd` file that only echoed its first argument. A host that passes user input to a tool's `.cmd` shim would run that user's commands.

When `FileName` names a batch file and `CommandLine` is null or empty, MiniPty starts the interpreter itself, with or without `Arguments`:

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Interpreter | `cmd.exe` from the system directory, never from `ComSpec`, run as `cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c ""script" args"`. `/d` skips the registry's AutoRun commands, `/v:OFF` keeps `!name!` from expanding, and `/e:ON` enables the extensions the percent escape needs. The registry can add AutoRun commands and change the other two defaults, so all three switches are explicit. `/c` strips the outer pair of quotes. |
| Quoting | An argument is quoted when it is empty, ends with a backslash, or contains any character other than an ASCII letter, an ASCII digit, or `#$*+-./:?@\_`. Every character `cmd.exe` treats specially is then inside quotes, and so is every non-ASCII space it splits a script's parameters on. A quote inside is doubled. Backslashes before a quote, and before the closing quote, are doubled. |
| Percent | Each `%`, in an argument or in the script path, is written as `%%cd:~,%`. `%cd:~,%` is an empty substring of the current directory, so the first `%` survives and no `%name%` expands. |
| Rejected | `ArgumentException` before anything starts, for an argument that contains a carriage return, a line feed, or a NUL, and for a file name that contains any of them or a quote. The full path the lookup produces is checked for the same characters and for a trailing backslash, since it joins the name with a `PATH` entry or the current directory that the name check never saw. `cmd.exe` drops a carriage return and ends its command line at a line feed or a NUL, so no quoting can deliver them. A command line longer than the 8191 characters `cmd.exe` runs is rejected the same way. It is counted as written, before any expansion: the program name, the switches, the script's full path, the quotes, and every escape (a `%` takes 8). Without the check the session would start and `cmd.exe` would fail with "The command line is too long". |
| Detection | By the extension of the name Windows opens: the last component left after `.` and `..` segments, with its trailing spaces and dots dropped. `script.cmd.`, `script.cmd\.`, and `script.cmd\sub\..` are batch files. A name such as `script.cmd\`, which no file matches, counts too, so its lookup fails instead of handing an unescaped line to `cmd.exe`. A file that starts with the `MZ` header is a program: `CreateProcess` runs it or refuses it, and never hands it to `cmd.exe`. It gets the file the lookup found as its application name, so it makes no second lookup that could find another file of the name, and a file that turns into a script between the header check and the start cannot reach `cmd.exe` with program quoting. An empty file fails with `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT`, and a file that cannot be opened as `CreateProcess` opens it fails with that error, such as `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` while another handle writes to it. |
| Lookup | The file `CreateProcess` would find for the name, found from the host's current directory and the host's `PATH`, or the child's `PATH` when `Environment` sets or removes it ([Program lookup](#program-lookup-windows)), never from the child's `WorkingDirectory`. A rooted name is taken as it is. A name that starts with `.\`, `..\`, `./`, or `../` is relative to the host's current directory. Any other name, with a directory part or without, is searched for in the host executable's directory, the host's current directory, the system directory, the 16-bit system directory, the Windows directory, and each `PATH` entry as written. The current directory is skipped when `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` is set and the name has no backslash. An empty `PATH` entry is the current directory unless it follows the last semicolon, a relative entry is relative to the current directory, and a quoted or padded entry matches nothing. The first match decides. A missing file fails with `Win32Exception` (`ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`), and a directory found first fails with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, as `CreateProcess` fails. `cmd.exe` receives the full path, so its own lookup (its working directory, then `PATH` with `PATHEXT`) does not run. |
| Delivered | Each argument is one parameter of the script (`%1`, `%2`, and so on). The script sees it as MiniPty wrote it: bare when it holds only the characters that need no quotes, otherwise quoted, with a quote inside doubled and the backslashes before a quote or the closing quote doubled. `%~1` drops only the outer quotes, so `C:\dir\` arrives there as `C:\dir\\`. A program the script forwards `%*` to, as tool shims do, receives each argument unchanged when it parses its command line with the UCRT, as .NET's apphost does. That was verified for quotes, backslashes, `%`, `!`, `& | < > ^ ( )`, `= , ;`, tabs, empty arguments, and non-ASCII text, also from a script under a directory named with a space, `&`, `%OS%`, `!`, parentheses, and `^`. `CommandLineToArgvW` and `msvcrt.dll` follow the pre-2008 rules, under which the argument boundaries after a doubled quote move. |
| Not covered | A raw `CommandLine` is passed unchanged, as its contract says, and `CreateProcess` starts `cmd.exe` for it with the registry's defaults, AutoRun included. A script that hands an argument to `cmd /c`, or uses it without its quotes as `%~1` in a command, can still be made to run something. Only the script can prevent that. Starting `cmd.exe` directly with `/c` and user input in `Arguments` is likewise `cmd.exe` parsing that input. |

Escaping was chosen over rejecting `cmd.exe`'s special characters: shims are called with paths, URLs, version ranges, and JSON, which contain `&`, `%`, `^`, and quotes, and the escaping above delivers all of them. Only the characters no quoting can deliver are rejected.

The doubled quote is a trade-off. `cmd.exe` toggles its quoting on every `"` and ignores the backslash before one, so a quote written as `\"` ends the quoting and `""` keeps it. The UCRT reads `""` inside quotes as one quote, but the pre-2008 parsers read it as a quote that also ends the quoting. Through a `%*` shim, a program that uses `CommandLineToArgvW` or `msvcrt.dll` then sees the argument boundaries after such an argument move. `a"b` alone arrives intact, but with `c` and `d` after it the three arrive as one argument, `a"b c d`, and `x" --evil "` arrives as three: `x"`, `--evil`, and `"`. For such a program that is an argument injection, not a command injection: user input with one quote can add a flag of its own. MiniPty cannot tell which parser the program behind a shim uses, and rejecting quotes would break JSON arguments to the UCRT programs that read them correctly, so the README tells a host that forwards user input to such a program to reject the quote itself.

## Program Lookup (Windows)

A `FileName` without a root, and without a leading `.\`, `..\`, `./`, or `../`, is searched for. On Unix the native shim resolves it against the child's final `PATH` before `execve` ([pty_crossplatform.md](../references/pty_crossplatform.md)). On Windows `CreateProcess` makes that search itself, from the host: its executable's directory, its current directory, the system directories, and the host's `PATH`. The environment block passed for the child plays no part, so a host that put a tool on the child's `PATH` could start it by name on Unix and not on Windows, where the spawn failed with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` although the child would have found the tool itself.

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| When | `Environment` sets or removes `PATH` (compared ignoring case, as Windows does). The child's `PATH` then differs from the host's, and MiniPty searches instead of `CreateProcess`. An overlay that leaves `PATH` alone changes nothing: the child's `PATH` is the host's, which `CreateProcess` searches as before, with no cost added to the spawn. |
| Where | The same places in the same order as `CreateProcess`, with the child's `PATH` entries in place of the host's: the host executable's directory, the host's current directory (skipped when `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` is set and the name has no backslash), the system directory, the 16-bit system directory, the Windows directory, then each fully qualified entry of the child's `PATH`, as written. A removed or empty `PATH` searches the fixed locations only, so `whoami` is still found in the system directory. The current directory is the host's, as for `CreateProcess`, not the child's `WorkingDirectory`. |
| Relative entries | An empty entry, `.`, and any relative, drive-relative (`C:dir`), or root-relative (`\dir`) entry of the child's `PATH` is skipped, where `CreateProcess` reads it against the current directory. `CreateProcess` does so even with `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` set: a program planted in the current directory ran for `;dir`, `.;dir`, `dir;;x`, and `dir\..` with the opt-out on. Applied to a `PATH` the caller wrote, that would start a program from the host's current directory, which is not the child's `WorkingDirectory` and which the caller cannot see, and would undo the opt-out; `extra + ";" + path` with an empty `extra` writes such an entry by accident. The child still receives its `PATH` unchanged and resolves its own commands by its own rules. |
| `.exe` | Appended when the last path component has no `.`, which is what `CreateProcess` does: `tool` finds only `tool.exe`, also when an extensionless `tool` sits beside it, and `sub\tool` and `sub.d\tool` find only `sub\tool.exe` and `sub.d\tool.exe`, although the documentation says a name with a path gets no extension. `tool.`, `tool.foo`, and `.tool` are taken as written, and Windows opens `tool.` as `tool`. `.com` and `PATHEXT` are not consulted, as `CreateProcess` does not consult them. |
| Batch shims | Written with their extension: `npm.cmd`, not `npm`. A name without one gets `.exe` and nothing else, with or without an overlay, so a tool installed as a `.cmd` or `.bat` shim (`npm`, `yarn`, `pnpm`, `code`) fails with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` when written bare. This is deliberate: a `FileName` that ends in `.bat` or `.cmd` is the one signal that the child is `cmd.exe` parsing a script, and it always takes the [Batch files](#batch-files-windows) path with its escaping. Resolving `PATHEXT` would let a bare name turn into a script that the caller never wrote, and would make the program depend on the order of directories and extensions; the caller who means a shim says so. |
| Started | The file found becomes `CreateProcessW`'s application name, so it makes no lookup of its own, and the command line keeps the name as given, so the child's `argv[0]` is unchanged. |
| Not searched | A rooted name, and one that starts with `.\`, `..\`, `./`, or `../`: `CreateProcess` does not search for these either, so they are left to it. A batch file follows the [Batch files](#batch-files-windows) rules with the child's `PATH` on the same condition; one started with a raw `CommandLine` stays with `CreateProcess`, which searches the host's `PATH`, because a script given as an application name has its command line rebuilt for `cmd.exe` with its quoting broken (measured: a quoted `argv[0]` made `cmd.exe` fail, and `"x y"` ran `x`). |
| Long paths | A rooted or dot-relative program path of 260 characters (`MAX_PATH`) or more becomes the application name too. `.exe` is appended by the rule above, and the file is checked first, so failures stay `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` and `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`. `CreateProcess`'s own lookup of such a command line fails from 260 characters (measured on Windows 11 26200: 259 starts, 260 fails), with `ERROR_FILENAME_EXCED_RANGE` even in a host that opted into long paths. The program starts only where the machine allows long paths (`LongPathsEnabled`) and the host's application manifest declares `longPathAware`. A .NET application host declares nothing by default, and `dotnet.exe` declares it. Elsewhere `Pty.Start` fails with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, as it did before. Shorter paths stay with `CreateProcess` and cost nothing more. Not covered: a `WorkingDirectory` of 260 characters or more, which `CreateProcess` refuses with `ERROR_DIRECTORY` in every host; a bare name that `CreateProcess` finds on a long `PATH` entry; and a batch file under a long path, which runs through `cmd.exe` as before and was not verified. |
| Failure | `Win32Exception` from `Pty.Start` before anything is created: `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` for a missing program, `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` for a directory of the name found first, as `CreateProcess` fails. |
| Trust | The overlay's `PATH` decides which program the host starts, as it already does on Unix and as it decides what the child runs afterwards. A host that builds `Environment` from a source it does not control, such as a workspace setting or a remote request, hands that source the choice of program: a writable fully qualified entry can supply any program the fixed locations do not hold first, and a UNC entry is probed from the host process, which authenticates to that server. The fixed locations come first, so a child `PATH` cannot replace a program in the host's directory or the system directories, such as `cmd.exe`. To pin the program, pass a full path in `FileName`. |
| Stream names | `x.cmd::$DATA` names the script's own content but does not end in `.cmd`, so it is not detected as a batch file. `CreateProcess` refuses it with `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT`, as a name it searches and as an application name, instead of starting `cmd.exe` with arguments quoted for a program, so it fails closed. A test pins that refusal. |

The rule is "sets or removes" rather than "differs from the host's" so that the behavior follows the overlay alone and not the host's environment at spawn time; an overlay that sets `PATH` to the host's own value goes through MiniPty's search, which finds the same file. Resolving every name in MiniPty was rejected: a spawn that inherits `PATH` would pay a path string allocation and a few probes for a result `CreateProcess` reaches anyway.

## Untrusted Program Names and Paths

MiniPty starts the program a name resolves to; it is not a sandbox. A host that builds `FileName`, an argument, or `WorkingDirectory` from input it does not control has to check what the operating system will resolve, not the string. These are the ways the two can differ:

| Case | What runs or is opened |
|---|---|
| `..` segments, trailing dots and spaces, `/` | Windows resolves `..` and drops trailing dots and spaces in each segment, as `Path.GetFullPath` does, so `C:\allowed\..\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe` is `cmd.exe`. This applies to a long path given as the application name too ([Program lookup](#program-lookup-windows)), which resolves exactly as the shorter path would. |
| A name relative to `.\` or `..\` | Relative to the host process's current directory, not to `WorkingDirectory`. That directory is process-wide state, which any thread can change. |
| A name that starts with `\\?\` | Taken without normalization, by Windows and by `Path.GetFullPath` alike. Such a name with backslashes starts the program it names, also as an application name, so a check must not assume that `..` in it was resolved. |
| A UNC name (`\\server\share\...`) | The host process opens it, and so connects and authenticates to that server, before the child starts. |
| A NUL | Rejected (see [Entry point](#entry-point)). Before that, `"...\cmd.exe\0C:\allowed\safe.exe"` started `cmd.exe` on Windows, and `"/bin/sh\0/usr/bin/safe"` started `/bin/sh` on Linux, while `Path.GetFileName` read `safe.exe` and `safe`. |
| A batch file | Its arguments are escaped for `cmd.exe` ([Batch files](#batch-files-windows)), but the script can still run what an argument holds. An alternate data stream such as `x.cmd::$DATA` is not a batch file and fails with `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT`. |

To check a program, resolve it with `Path.GetFullPath` and compare the result with the programs you allow, or with an allowed directory followed by its separator, so that `C:\allowed-but-not` does not pass for `C:\allowed`. Pass that full path as `FileName`, so that the current directory cannot change it after the check.

## Spawn Environment

`PtyStartInfo.Environment` is an overlay on top of the parent process environment, not a replacement block.

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `Environment = null` | Inherit the parent environment. |
| `Environment["KEY"] = "value"` | Set or override `KEY` for the child. |
| `Environment["KEY"] = null` | Remove `KEY` from the child environment. Removing a missing key succeeds. |
| `Environment["KEY"] = ""` | Set an empty value on platforms that preserve empty environment variables. Windows children observe empty entries as missing. |

Environment keys are case-insensitive on Windows and case-sensitive on Unix. Invalid names are rejected at spawn time: empty names, names containing `=`, and names or values containing NUL are invalid. Duplicate-equivalent overlay keys are resolved by enumeration order; the last value wins.

On Unix, MiniPty removes inherited terminal-container and size variables before applying the explicit overlay: `TMUX`, `TMUX_PANE`, `STY`, `WINDOW`, `WINDOWID`, `TERMCAP`, `COLUMNS`, and `LINES`. This prevents a fresh PTY from inheriting stale parent terminal state. Because sanitize runs before the overlay, callers can still explicitly pass any of these variables.

On Unix, `TerminalName` sets `TERM` after the environment overlay. If `TerminalName` is null or empty and no `TERM` remains, MiniPty sets `TERM=xterm-256color` unless `TERM` was explicitly removed by the overlay. `Environment["TERM"] = ""` is respected as an explicit empty value on Unix. On Windows, `TerminalName` does not set `TERM`; use `Environment["TERM"]` to pass it explicitly.

MiniPty environment inheritance follows normal process-spawn behavior and is not a sandbox. Callers exposing PTYs to untrusted users must isolate the child process outside MiniPty, for example with OS users, containers, sandboxing, or explicit environment removal.

## Process Tree

By default, ending a session on Windows ends the child and the processes attached to its pseudo-console. A descendant in a console of its own, or a GUI program, keeps running, and when the host process crashes every descendant does ([Descendants](lifecycle.md#descendants)).

`PtyStartInfo.KillProcessTree = true` runs the child in a job object with kill-on-close. The child joins it at creation, and its descendants inherit it. It joins through `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST` in the same attribute list as the pseudo-console, not by starting suspended and being assigned, so there is no instant in which a fast child exits or starts a descendant outside the job. ConPTY's console host is created before the child and is not in the job; it ends when the pseudo-console closes, as it does without the option.

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Ends the tree | `Dispose`, `Kill` (also after the child itself has exited), and the end of the host process in any way, including a crash: the kernel closes the job's only handle. |
| Leaves it running | The child's own exit. The session owns the tree until it is disposed, so a descendant of a finished child runs until then. |
| Breakaway | Not allowed. A program that asks to leave the job (`CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB`) fails to start in the session. |
| Host inside a job | Supported: jobs nest, as under CI runners and editors. |
| Failure | A job that cannot be created fails `Pty.Start`; there is no fallback to a session without it. |
| Unix | Ignored. Disposal hangs the child up as without it. |

The option is off by default because it also ends programs the user started from the terminal on purpose, such as an editor window.

## Inherited Cursor

ConPTY keeps its own screen buffer and starts by assuming that the frontend's screen is empty. By default the in-box ConPTY's first output clears the screen and homes the cursor (`ESC[2J ESC[H`; the out-of-band host measured does not, see [Out-of-band ConPTY](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#out-of-band-conpty)), which erases whatever the frontend showed before the child started: an editor's banner written ahead of the shell (VS Code's `initialText`), or the prompt and earlier lines of the terminal a console host runs in. A Unix PTY passes bytes through without a screen model, so the child simply continues at the frontend's cursor.

`PtyStartInfo.InheritCursor = true` gives Windows the Unix behavior. ConPTY is created with `PSEUDOCONSOLE_INHERIT_CURSOR`, asks the frontend for the cursor position (`ESC[6n`) as its first output, and continues from the reported position without clearing. The option is off by default because it needs an answer:

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Answer | The frontend writes a cursor position report (`ESC[row;columnR`) to the session input. Terminal emulators (xterm.js, VS Code, Windows Terminal) do this on their own; with [Console](console.md) attach, the host terminal answers and the input pump forwards the answer, provided `Attach` runs before the output pump writes the query. |
| Until answered | The child stalls whether or not it writes: the frontend sees only the query, and a child that writes nothing does not get on with its work either. The in-box ConPTY has no timeout; the out-of-band host stops waiting after 1 s and runs the child. A late answer resumes the child normally. |
| Input until answered | Held in order, not dropped, and delivered after the answer (measured on the in-box host). A Ctrl+C the user types at what looks like a hang therefore ends the child once the answer arrives, before it has printed anything. |
| The report | Consumed by ConPTY; the child never reads it. A second report after the first was consumed too, by both hosts, for a child reading line input. |
| Never answered | `Kill` and `Dispose` still end the session and its output. As the session ends, the in-box host emits the startup it skipped, clear screen (`ESC[2J`) included, so a frontend that renders that output loses the screen the option was meant to keep. |
| Output-only consumers | `CompleteAsync`, Capture, and similar consumers that never write input must leave it off, or write a report themselves. |

[InheritCursorWait.cs](../../../samples/SingleFiles/InheritCursorWait.cs) prints each of these cases as a timeline, on the in-box and the out-of-band ConPTY.

## Out-of-band ConPTY

Windows ships ConPTY in `kernel32.dll`, backed by the `conhost.exe` of the user's Windows build. That host renders the child's output and decides which VT sequences reach the frontend. The builds measured (Windows 11 26100 and 26200) drop graphics protocols (Sixel, Kitty) and the OSC 11 and XTGETTCAP queries, answer device attributes, cursor position, and DECRQSS queries from their own state instead of asking the frontend, reorder forwarded sequences relative to text, and expose no clear operation. Mouse tracking modes (1000, 1003, 1006) and DECCKM reach the frontend only when the child has switched its console input to VT (`ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT`, measured on 26200), and a child that reads Win32 mouse events gets mouse reporting requested for it. A terminal emulator on the in-box ConPTY therefore cannot show images or answer color queries, and its behavior changes with Windows updates. Nothing MiniPty can pass or call changes that: the other `CreatePseudoConsole` flag bits tried left the output unchanged, and `kernel32.dll` exports no clear ([reference](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#out-of-band-conpty)).

Microsoft publishes the implementation Windows Terminal carries as the NuGet package `Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY`: `conpty.dll` plus `OpenConsole.exe`, one host process per session like the in-box one. MiniPty ships neither file and takes no dependency on the package; an application that wants it brings its own, and nothing changes for applications that do not.

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Opt-in | The application references the package, loads the DLL with `ConPtyLibrary.Load(absolutePath)` or `ConPtyLibrary.TryLoadFromApplicationDirectory()`, and sets `PtyStartInfo.ConPty`. Per session, so a process can run both implementations and a host can say which one a session used. Never detected and never process-wide: a package that arrives transitively must not change which console host every session in the process runs on, and a process-wide setting would also hide which implementation a given session ran on. |
| Loading | By absolute path only; a bare name would be searched for along the loader's path and could bind a copy of `conpty.dll` an operating system ships. One instance per path, loaded for the process lifetime. The contract is the DLL's exports, not its version: `Load` resolves the five functions MiniPty calls (`ConptyCreatePseudoConsole`, `ConptyResizePseudoConsole`, `ConptyClosePseudoConsole`, `ConptyReleasePseudoConsole`, `ConptyClearPseudoConsole`) and throws `EntryPointNotFoundException` when one is missing. `FileVersion` is reported for diagnostics. |
| The host | `conpty.dll` launches `OpenConsole.exe` from beside itself, or from a subdirectory named after the operating system's architecture; when neither exists it launches the in-box `conhost.exe` instead, without an error. `ConPtyLibrary.HasConsoleHost` reports that probe before the first spawn. MiniPty's `buildTransitive` targets stage the host beside `conpty.dll` in a consumer's output, in both the runtime-specific and the portable layout, when the package is referenced (`MiniPtyStageConPtyHost=false` disables it). |
| Flags | None are passed beyond `InheritCursor`; the other flag bits have changed meaning between package versions. |
| End of output | After the child is attached, MiniPty releases its reference to the console server (`ConptyReleasePseudoConsole`), so the host exits with its last client and the output pipe breaks: output ends on the pipe break, 2–3 ms after exit measured. Resize and clear keep working, as they use the signal pipe. The in-box ConPTY does the same from Windows 11 24H2 (build 26100), whose `kernel32.dll` exports `ReleasePseudoConsole`; on older builds an in-box session's output ends only on the drain's close, after the 100 ms post-exit quiet interval. |
| Startup query | The host asks the frontend what terminal it is (`ESC[c`, Primary Device Attributes) when the session starts, and consumes the first answer. A terminal emulator answers on its own; MiniPty never answers for it, because a second answer reaches the child as keystrokes. With the verified package version the host does not wait for the answer unless `InheritCursor` is set; versions before 1.25 waited 3 s per session for it. |
| Queries from the child | Forwarded to the frontend, never answered by the host: a child that asks for the cursor position or device attributes waits for the frontend's answer. The in-box host answers those itself, so a read-only consumer (`CompleteAsync`, Capture) of such a child is better served by the in-box ConPTY. |
| `Clear()` | `PtySession.Clear()` and `PtyTerminal.Clear()` clear the host's buffer (`ConptyClearPseudoConsole`, cursor to the top). The host emits nothing for it, as the frontend has already cleared its own display; the next output is placed at row 1. A no-op on the in-box ConPTY and on Unix. |
| Verified version | `1.25.260930003`, pinned for the repository's tests and Windows samples only (`Directory.Packages.props`). Any published version loads; 1.25 is the recommended floor because of the startup query. |
| Trust | `Load` runs native code with the process's token, and the DLL launches the host beside itself with a full path (never a search): the trust boundary is the directory the two files live in, the same one the application's own binaries live in. The application passes only paths it controls; a path on a network share or removable media is accepted rather than rejected, because an application running from such a place loads its own code from there too; `TryLoadFromApplicationDirectory` probes nothing outside the application directory; the staging targets act only on the DLL resolved from the `Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY` package. The package's `conpty.dll` and `OpenConsole.exe` are Authenticode-signed by Microsoft, and `conpty.dll` imports only Windows API sets, so no dependent DLL can be planted beside it. No token, user, or privilege is involved: `ConptyCreatePseudoConsoleAsUser` is not exposed. |
| Unix | A `ConPtyLibrary` cannot be loaded; `Load` throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` and `TryLoadFromApplicationDirectory` returns null. |

MiniPty ships no binary because it cannot guarantee the host's placement in every consumer's output layout (the package's own build files place it only for a direct, architecture-specific reference, so a .NET project gets `conpty.dll` and no host), because the version and its security updates belong to the application, and because most consumers, which only read output, do not need a 1 MB host process.

## Session Contract

| Member | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `Input` / `Output` | Raw byte streams. No line-ending translation. stdout and stderr are merged on `Output`. `Output` is a view over the session's output buffer: `ReadAsync` never blocks the calling thread; `Read` blocks, per the `Stream` contract. |
| `ReadOutputAsync` | Persistent bytes-only output streaming. Returns `IAsyncEnumerable<PtyOutputChunk>`. |
| `WriteInputAsync` | Writes UTF-8 text by default, or raw bytes. Does not close stdin. Never blocks the calling thread: bytes the terminal accepts at once are written synchronously (the usual case, allocation-free after the session's first write), and the rest is written in order in the background: on Unix by the I/O loop as the child reads, on Windows by I/O completions as ConPTY takes input again. Writes reach the child in issue order, and `SendEof` takes effect after every write issued before it. A canceled token, a closed input, and a failed write are reported through the returned task rather than thrown from the call. Canceling a waiting write discards the bytes not yet handed to the terminal. Those already handed over still arrive, which on Windows include a pending part of up to 4 KiB that ConPTY has not read yet. |
| `SendEof()` | Signals end of stdin using platform-specific behavior. See [Lifecycle](lifecycle.md). |
| `Resize(PtySize)` / `Resize(PtySize, PtyPixelSize?)` | Resizes after spawn; Unix also reports optional pixel dimensions, while Windows ignores pixels. Child exit never makes it fail: while the transport is open the size is applied, and once the transport has been closed after exit the call is a no-op that keeps `Size`. On Windows from 11 24H2, and with the out-of-band ConPTY, the console host ends with its last client, 2–5 ms after the child unless a grandchild stays attached, and a resize after that is the same no-op while the transport has yet to close. Only disposal (`ObjectDisposedException`), invalid pixel dimensions, and an OS failure while the child is running throw. A running child is notified as on a terminal: `SIGWINCH` on Unix, and on Windows a `WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT` input record for a child that enabled window input. |
| `Clear()` | Clears the pseudo-console's screen buffer for a frontend that cleared its own display. Effective on Windows with an out-of-band ConPTY ([Out-of-band ConPTY](#out-of-band-conpty)); a no-op on the in-box ConPTY, on Unix, and once the transport has been closed after exit. Throws only after disposal and when the OS call fails while the child is running. |
| `WaitForExitAsync` | Waits for child exit and returns `PtyExitStatus` (exit code plus Unix termination signal). Cancellation stops waiting only; the child keeps running. Without a cancelable token every call returns the same task, so repeated waits allocate nothing. Disposal before the exit has been observed fails the wait with `ObjectDisposedException`, and a call made after disposal throws it. A wait started earlier still reports the status of a child whose exit was observed before disposal; after disposal, read `ExitStatus` instead. |
| `CompleteAsync` | Convenience API for one-shot input, wait, drain, and result materialization. See [Completion](completion.md). |
| `Kill()` | Terminates the child process without releasing handles. |
| `Kill(PtySignal)` | Sends a signal on Unix, through the child's pidfd on Linux when the kernel provides one, and otherwise with `kill(2)` once a check shows the pid is still an unreaped child. No signal is sent once MiniPty has reaped the child. Without a pidfd, another child of the host that got the pid after other code reaped the child would receive it. The child may handle or ignore catchable signals. On Windows the signal is advisory and the child is terminated (node-pty parity). Undefined enum values throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` on both platforms. |
| `HasExited` / `ExitCode?` | Reports the exit observed by the background exit watcher; reading it never blocks or reaps. `ExitCode` is null until the child has exited. On Unix the watcher keeps observing after disposal, so a child disposed while running reports what ended it: its own exit, 129 (`SIGHUP`), or 137 (`SIGKILL` after the grace period). |
| `ExitStatus?` | `PtyExitStatus` after exit; null before. |
| `ActiveProcessName` | Foreground process name for editor title polling on Unix; null when unavailable and on Windows. |
| `Dispose` / `DisposeAsync` | Ends the child if still running and releases handles without blocking. On Unix the child is hung up first (`SIGHUP`, the signal a shell receives when its terminal window closes, so it saves its history). The signal is sent on the disposing thread without blocking. The terminal's master stays open until the child is reaped or killed, so that hang-up is the only one the child gets while it runs, which lets a shell save its history and hang up its jobs. Its output is discarded meanwhile. A child that has not exited one second later is killed by the background exit watcher, and if the process exits normally before then (returns from `Main` or calls `Environment.Exit`), the kill is sent at exit. A host ended within that second by a crash or by a signal it does not cancel, such as `SIGTERM` to a console app, never sends the kill, so a child that ignores the hang-up survives. Calling `Kill()` first ends such a child at once but skips the hang-up. An interactive shell killed this way cannot resend the hang-up to its jobs, so a running background job keeps running. A host can instead cancel such a signal, end its sessions as in the app-exit row of [GUI hosts](#gui-hosts), and exit normally. The kills are then sent at exit. MiniPty signals only the child. When it exits, the system hangs up the terminal's foreground process group, so a descendant in that group ends too unless it ignores `SIGHUP`. On Windows it is terminated, and closing the pseudo-console ends every process attached to it; a descendant in a console of its own keeps running. In-flight output reads and exit waits fail with `ObjectDisposedException`. `DisposeAsync` also completes once background output reading has stopped; every call waits, including one after `Dispose` and concurrent ones. Output chunk memory is invalid after either. Safe to call more than once and from several threads at once: the first call tears down, and handles are released exactly once. |

## Exit Status

`PtyExitStatus` reports `ExitCode` and `Signal`:

- `ExitCode` always equals `PtySession.ExitCode`. On Unix a signal-terminated child keeps MiniPty's existing `128 + signal` mapping (for example 143 for SIGTERM) — deliberately not node-pty's 0-on-signal, so a killed child never reads as success and there is one exit-code story across the library.
- `NodePtyExitCode` projects that status into node-pty's frontend shape: zero when `Signal` is present, otherwise `ExitCode`. Terminal bridges use this projection without changing core completion semantics.
- `Signal` is the raw OS signal number (`waitpid` `WTERMSIG`), null on normal exit and when the wait status was lost (ECHILD reap-lost path). Windows never reports a signal.
- `PtySignal` members are logical identifiers mapped to native numbers per platform (SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2 numbering differs between Linux and macOS/FreeBSD); reporting uses raw OS numbers.

## Embedder Patterns

MiniPty core is the PTY transport for multiple embedder shapes ([spec.md](../spec.md)). The core API is unchanged; patterns differ by who reads output and who writes input.

| Use case | Output consumer (exactly one) | Input source | Packages |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — General transport** | Embedder (`ReadOutputAsync` or raw `Output`) | Embedder (`WriteInputAsync`) | **MiniPty** |
| **2 — One-shot record** | `PtyCapture.RunAsync` (completion sink fed as output is read) | `PtyCompleteOptions` / capture options | **MiniPty.Capture** |
| **3 — Interactive host** | Embedder `ReadOutputAsync` (record + write host `stdout`) | **MiniPty.Console** host keyboard + optional embedder writes | **MiniPty** + **MiniPty.Console** |
| **4 — Editor terminal** | **MiniPty.Terminal** `PtyTerminal` (owns `ReadOutputAsync`) | Frontend key events → bridge → `WriteInputAsync` | **MiniPty** + **MiniPty.Terminal** |

**Use case 3** does not add a second PTY output reader. [Console](console.md) configures the host terminal and forwards host stdin bytes; the embedder keeps the single `ReadOutputAsync` enumeration for PTY → host display and recording.

**Use case 4** does not use **MiniPty.Console** (no host console attach). The push facade, flow control, and WebSocket bridge live in [Terminal](terminal.md).

## Backpressure

A PTY has backpressure. Each session reads its output from spawn into a bounded buffer, and the session's single output consumer drains it. On Windows the reads are overlapped and complete on a completion port of MiniPty's own, which one background thread waits on for every session, so a session holds no thread, and holds no buffer while nothing is unread; on Unix one background loop, the exit watcher's thread, reads every session's output from its non-blocking master (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and FreeBSD), so a session there holds no thread or idle buffer either. A Unix master that loop cannot register, which happens only without epoll or kqueue or at a kernel watch limit such as Linux's `fs.epoll.max_user_watches`, fails `Pty.Start` with `IOException`: nothing else would read the session. A plain `ReadOutputAsync` consumer on Linux and macOS also reads the master on its own thread while output keeps coming, so a flood it keeps up with wakes no other thread per chunk; on macOS, where the master holds 1 KiB and the child refills it only after each read, that consumer also waits for the master on its own thread, for up to a millisecond before it parks, while the child streams (a read that filled the master starts that, a wait that brings nothing ends it), on a kqueue of the session's own, which is one more descriptor per such session. A consumer on a UI thread never waits there. A failure to open the epoll or kqueue itself fails only the starts that meet it, since each later start tries to open it again. When the buffer is full, reading stops and the OS PTY buffer fills, so a child whose output nobody reads still blocks eventually. Callers must use `ReadOutputAsync`, `CompleteAsync`, `PtyCapture.RunAsync`, or continuously read `Output` themselves.

Reading from spawn means early output is never stranded: a child does not stall on its first writes before a consumer attaches, and output produced before the consumer starts is delivered first.

`ReadOutputAsync` is the supported high-level persistent output API. It is bytes-only and performs no text decoding. It does not drop data.

`PtyOutputChunk.Data` is ephemeral: it is valid only until the next successful `MoveNextAsync` call on the same enumeration, or until the session is disposed. Callers that need to retain bytes must copy them before advancing the reader. Chunks are handed out in place from the buffer and the enumerator is reused per session, so enumeration allocates nothing per chunk.

Only one output consumer is active per session (see [Lifecycle](lifecycle.md#output-consumer-exclusivity)). A concurrent reader attempt throws `InvalidOperationException`.

Managed buffering is bounded by the buffer's capacity (currently 16 KiB). Each read is published as it completes, with no window: batching comes from the consumer's pace instead, so a consumer still busy with its previous chunk takes everything that arrived meanwhile as one chunk. A chunk is all the contiguous output published when the consumer asks for it, up to the end of the buffer: a consumer that keeps up gets each piece as it is published, and one that fell behind, such as a WebSocket still sending the previous chunk, gets several pieces as one chunk. Reading stops while less than 4 KiB is free. Output that fills the buffer while nobody reads it holds back the rest, so such a session may not reach end of output after exit until a consumer reads, and the consumer then gets all of it; a few small frames no longer fill it. On macOS the child's exit itself waits for that read when its last output is still in the terminal, because macOS would otherwise discard it 0.6 s after the exit. The capacity and the maximum chunk size are implementation details and may change. One-shot `CompleteAsync` and `PtyCapture.RunAsync` are the exception by design: their result holds the whole output, so it grows with it.

## Caller Context

Asynchronous members never block the calling thread and never run library code on the caller's `SynchronizationContext`, so they can be awaited from a UI thread. Only the caller's own continuation resumes on its captured context, and only when the operation had to wait; `ConfigureAwait(false)` opts out as usual.

| Member | Behavior on the caller's thread |
|---|---|
| `ReadOutputAsync`, `Output.ReadAsync` | Complete synchronously while output is buffered; otherwise resume when output arrives. Under a `SynchronizationContext` or a non-default `TaskScheduler`, a read that would complete synchronously after 8 ms of reads that all did completes through that context instead, once, so the dispatcher runs its queue before the consumer resumes. |
| `WaitForExitAsync` | Awaits the exit watcher's notification. |
| `CompleteAsync`, `PtyCapture.RunAsync` | Output is collected as it is read (the I/O loop on Windows, the watcher loop on Unix); the caller awaits the input write, exit, and end of output. `Input`, when set, is written as by `WriteInputAsync`. |
| `DisposeAsync` | Returns at once and completes when output reading has stopped, for every caller. |
| `Output.Read`, `Input.Write` | Block, per the `Stream` contract. |
| `WriteInputAsync` | Completes at once when the terminal takes the bytes; otherwise when the rest has been written in the background. That happens when the terminal's input buffer is full: on Unix when the child has not read the tty input queue, and on Windows when ConPTY has not read the 4 KiB input pipe, which it stops reading while output nobody reads has backed up. A macOS tty in canonical mode holds back a write only while a complete line is queued. Once 1,024 bytes of a line are pending, later bytes are dropped, and the write still completes (see [macOS line limit](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#unix-stdin-eof)). |

Shapes rejected for this contract:

- **Replacing `Task.Yield` with a switch to the thread pool.** It fixed the UI freezes with the smallest change, but kept a pool hop and an allocation per read, two parked pool workers per idle session, and three separate transport read paths plus two drain paths.
- **`System.IO.Pipelines` `PipeReader` as the output API.** It ships with the shared framework and batches naturally, but `ReadOnlySequence` and `AdvanceTo(consumed, examined)` are easy to misuse, and awaiting `FlushAsync` from the output driver allocates. A byte ring that hands out one contiguous chunk at a time batches the same way and is simpler inside and out.
- **Windows input through non-blocking (`PIPE_NOWAIT`) writes with a retry.** Nothing signals when ConPTY reads input again, so the retry would poll.
- **A Windows input writer thread.** One per session costs the thread per session that the output engines avoid, and one shared writer would stall behind any session whose ConPTY stopped reading.

## GUI Hosts

A desktop terminal control (WinUI, WPF, WinForms, Avalonia) can drive a session entirely from its UI thread. The caller-context contract above is what makes that safe; this section is the recommended shape.

| Host concern | Recommended pattern | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ConPTY (Windows) | Reference the `Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY` package and start every session with `ConPty = ConPtyLibrary.TryLoadFromApplicationDirectory()`. Log `HasConsoleHost` and `FileVersion`; `HasConsoleHost` false means `OpenConsole.exe` was not staged | The in-box ConPTY drops graphics protocols and some terminal queries, forwards mouse tracking only for programs that read VT input, and changes with Windows updates ([Out-of-band ConPTY](#out-of-band-conpty)). The out-of-band implementation forwards them, supports `Clear()`, and ends output as soon as the child exits on every Windows build (the in-box one does from Windows 11 24H2). Without a staged host it silently runs on the in-box `conhost.exe`. `TryLoadFromApplicationDirectory` returns null on Unix and when the DLL is not staged, so the same line works on every platform and falls back to the in-box ConPTY |
| Output | `await foreach (var chunk in session.ReadOutputAsync())` in the UI thread's own async method, decoding each chunk in place with an incremental `Decoder` (a chunk can split a multi-byte sequence) | `MoveNextAsync` never blocks, and when it waits the continuation resumes on the dispatcher, so the chunk is processed on the UI thread with no copy and no marshaling. The chunk is valid until the next `MoveNextAsync`; copy it only if it must outlive that. A handler slower than the child's output always finds the next chunk buffered, so after 8 ms of synchronous chunks the next one is delivered through the dispatcher: input and rendering keep running during a flood, and nothing is needed in the loop for it |
| Push transports | `PtyTerminal` from **MiniPty.Terminal** | Its handlers run on background threads: marshal to the dispatcher and copy any bytes the UI retains |
| Input | `await session.WriteInputAsync(...)` from key handlers | Completes at once when the terminal takes the bytes, otherwise in the background; never blocks the UI thread |
| Layout | `session.Resize(...)` from size-changed events, at any time | Dimensions clamp to the platform limit, a zero-sized window before layout clamps to 1×1, and a resize after child exit and transport close is a no-op |
| Exit | `await session.WaitForExitAsync()` (or `PtyTerminal.Completion`) | Completes from the exit watcher, and the wait holds no thread. Disposing the session before the child exits, as a tab close does, fails this wait with `ObjectDisposedException`, so a host that keeps such a wait running catches it |
| Tab close | `await session.DisposeAsync()`; `Dispose()` when nothing can be awaited | Neither blocks; `DisposeAsync` also completes once background output reading has stopped. On Unix the shell is hung up and gets a one-second grace while the host keeps running |
| App exit | In a shutdown step the app waits for: `session.Kill(PtySignal.Hangup)`, then `await session.WaitForExitAsync(token)` with a timeout, catching the `OperationCanceledException` the timeout throws, with `DisposeAsync()` in `finally` (or `await using`) so it runs either way. With several tabs, hang up every session first and wait for all of them under one timeout | Disposal's grace ends when the process exits, because the pending kill is sent at exit. Hanging up and waiting first gives the shell its time to save history before the app goes away. The dispose must still run: a session that is never disposed gets no kill at exit, so a child that ignores the hang-up would outlive the app. Where the close handler cannot be awaited, dispose at once instead, as the samples do. On Windows `Kill` terminates at once |
| Many tabs | Nothing to do | No session blocks a thread-pool worker, so idle tabs do not starve the host's pool. An idle tab holds no thread and no output buffer: on each OS one loop serves every session |

Hosts that keep sessions in a non-UI context should know that, with no `SynchronizationContext` current, a waiting `MoveNextAsync` resumes through the thread pool like any other `await`; a host that blocks many pool workers (for example in `Process.WaitForExit`) delays those resumptions along with everything else in the process.

[samples/WinUiTerminal](../../../samples/WinUiTerminal) (code-only WinUI 3, Windows) and [samples/AvaloniaTerminal](../../../samples/AvaloniaTerminal) (Avalonia; Windows, Linux, macOS) are terminal emulators on one shared VT parser and screen buffer, [samples/TerminalEmulator](../../../samples/TerminalEmulator), that follow this table with no `Task.Run`; only the drawing and input layer differs between them. Each sample has a single window, whose close ends the app, so they dispose at once on close (the Tab close row) rather than hanging up and waiting first. Why they are built this way, and what building them taught, is in [gui_terminal_samples.md](../references/gui_terminal_samples.md).

## Lessons Learned

- The textbook glibc `WIFSIGNALED` macro relies on a signed-char cast that a direct C# transcription loses, misclassifying the stopped marker `0x7f` as signaled. Unreachable because MiniPty never asks for stopped children (no `WUNTRACED`), but load-bearing once the termination signal became public API, so the managed decoder used the explicit `(status & 0x7f) != 0 && (status & 0x7f) != 0x7f` form. Decoding has since moved into the native shim, which uses the platform's own macros, or the `waitid` siginfo when it reaps through a pidfd on Linux.
- Environment overlay is safer for MiniPty than node-pty-style replacement because Windows child startup is fragile when inherited variables such as `SystemRoot` are accidentally omitted.
- Unix terminal-size variables such as `COLUMNS` and `LINES` can make a fresh PTY behave like the parent terminal. Sanitizing them before overlay avoids stale child-visible terminal state.
- Windows does not preserve empty environment variables as child-visible empty values. MiniPty keeps the API distinction so Unix can express empty values, but Windows children observe them like missing variables.
- A fixed public buffer capacity is a poor contract for `ReadOutputAsync`: it turns an allocation/backpressure tuning knob into observable API surface. The stable contract is bounded no-drop streaming with producer wait; capacity should remain internal unless a future options API exposes it deliberately.
- On Windows ConPTY, `PeekNamedPipe` often reports zero pending bytes even when more output is in flight. The reader thread therefore appended to a slot with non-blocking continuation reads (`PIPE_NOWAIT`) within a short micro-window before publishing it, so bulk output batched without delaying the first byte of interactive output. The completion driver that replaced it publishes each read and leaves batching to the consumer, and the window went with the reader threads.
- Kill-on-cancellation must not rely on a token registration made alongside `WaitAsync(token)`. `CancellationTokenSource` runs callbacks in reverse registration order, so `WaitAsync`'s callback resumes the waiter first, and the waiter's cleanup unregisters the kill callback before it runs. The waiter kills in its own cancellation handler instead.
- Completing a consumer wait can throw. A wait completes by posting the consumer's continuation to its captured context, on the output driver's thread (then a reader thread, now an I/O completion or the I/O loop), a disposing thread, or a canceling (possibly timer) thread; a context whose `Post` throws (a UI dispatcher already shut down) crashed the process from the reader or timer thread. Every completion of an output wait swallows that exception, because that continuation can never run. Task-based waits such as `WaitForExitAsync` follow the BCL, which rethrows it on the thread pool and still terminates the process.
- An exit listener must be set with a full fence. The session sets the listener and then checks for an exit that happened earlier, while the watcher records exit and then reads the listener; with release/acquire ordering both sides missed each other on Apple Silicon in a litmus test, and the post-exit drain was never scheduled.
- A consumer wait must be completed outside the lock that guards its state. Completing it under the lock runs the consumer's continuation inline, and that continuation's `CancellationTokenRegistration.Dispose` blocks until a concurrently running cancellation callback returns, while the callback blocks on the lock. The output pump claims a wait with a compare-and-swap and completes it without holding any lock.
- Resize must tolerate child exit. GUI hosts forward layout changes asynchronously to child exit, so a size change can arrive after post-exit drain has closed the transport; throwing there terminated WinUI hosts from a size-changed handler. Defining the no-op by transport state rather than by `HasExited` keeps resize-after-fast-exit working while the transport is still open, and on Windows a reference on the pseudo-console handle keeps a concurrent drain close from invalidating it mid-call. An open transport does not mean a live console host, though: once MiniPty releases the host at spawn, it ends 2–5 ms after the child, `ResizePseudoConsole` then fails, and the resize is skipped. `PtyResizeAfterExitWithOpenTransportDoesNotThrow` assumed the host lived until the close, and failed in about one of four loaded full runs, whenever its thread resized 5 ms or more after the exit; a grandchild now keeps the host alive for it.
- Pixel dimensions fit Unix's 16-bit `winsize` fields. MiniPty clamps larger caller values to `ushort.MaxValue`; zero remains a valid "unknown" pixel dimension.
- The in-box ConPTY's inherit-cursor wait is unbounded. Measured on Windows 11 build 26200: without an answer to `ESC[6n`, `cmd /c echo` had not exited after 15 s; an answer sent after 3 s resumed it at once. Out-of-band ConPTY 1.25 bounds a related startup wait to 1 s ([reference](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#out-of-band-conpty)), so the in-box behavior must not be assumed from the redistributable's source. This is why the option stays opt-in rather than defaulting on for terminal frontends.
- The inherit-cursor wait holds the whole child, not only its output, and holds input rather than dropping it. "A child that writes stalls" was the first description; rerun on build 26200 with [InheritCursorWait.cs](../../../samples/SingleFiles/InheritCursorWait.cs), `cmd /c ping -n 3 127.0.0.1 >nul` had not started `ping` after 3 s and `cmd.exe` used no CPU after its first 16 ms; a Ctrl+C written 1 s into the wait did nothing, then ended the child with `0xC000013A` the moment an answer arrived 2 s later; and `Kill` during the wait made the in-box host emit its clear (`ESC[2J`) as the session ended. To the user it is a blank terminal that ignores Ctrl+C, and the Ctrl+C takes effect later.
- MiniPty does not answer the cursor query on the frontend's behalf after a timeout, though a duplicate report proved harmless where measured: a second report written 500 ms after the first did not reach a `cmd` `set /p` child on either host (3 of 3 runs each), and the out-of-band host also consumed one arriving after its own 1 s wait. A child that reads VT input was not measured. The reason is the position: MiniPty does not know where the frontend's cursor is, and a made-up position puts the host's screen model out of step with the frontend's display, the mismatch the option exists to avoid. A frontend that cannot answer leaves the option off.
- What the in-box host forwards depends on the child's console input mode. The first VT probe child left its input in the default mode, and "the in-box ConPTY never forwards mouse tracking" was concluded from it; rerun on build 26200 with `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT` set, the same mouse modes and DECCKM were forwarded, and a child that enabled Win32 mouse input made the host request `ESC[?1003;1006h` itself. A probe of a console host states the child's input mode and varies it, and checks what the child receives back as well as what reaches the frontend: the in-box host answered DA1, DECRQSS, and cursor position queries itself, which forwarding alone does not show. That rerun also recorded the forwarded modes as "in order with text", though only line breaks separated the sequences, so their order against text could not show; with text written between the sequences, the in-box host sent the modes ahead of text the child had written before them. A probe that checks order puts distinct text between the sequences.
- The in-box host cannot be brought closer to the out-of-band one from MiniPty. Measured on build 26200 (conhost `10.0.26100.1`) with a raw ConPTY probe: the flag bits older headers name resize-quirk (0x2), Win32 input mode (0x4), and passthrough (0x8), and 0x10 and 0x18, were each accepted and changed no byte of the output beyond the per-session `id` in re-encoded OSC 8 links, with either console input mode, so there is no passthrough mode to enable. The host does act on the clear signal that `conpty.dll` writes to the pseudo-console's signal pipe, but `kernel32.dll` exposes no function for it; reaching the pipe needs the layout of the opaque `HPCON` and the signal's packet format, neither documented, and a host that does not know the signal was not measured, so `Clear()` stays a no-op in-box rather than depending on either. The one documented lever found is `STARTUPINFO.lpTitle`: left unset, as MiniPty leaves it, the in-box host announces the program's path as the window title; set empty, it announces none, as the out-of-band host, and titles the child sets still pass. Setting it would remove the title in-box frontends show today. Applications that need the out-of-band behavior use the out-of-band ConPTY.
- The in-box `ReleasePseudoConsole` is looked up at run time, not imported, because builds before Windows 11 24H2 lack it and an import would throw on every session there. A lookup that fails falls back to the slower drain without any error, so the end-of-output test probes the export on its own and, wherever the export exists, requires that output ended without the drain's close. It first required a median exit-to-end latency under 50 ms instead; that caught the call being removed (112–118 ms), but under 1.5× CPU oversubscription it failed with the release in place, because the two continuations it timed were each delayed by up to about 140 ms, and the exit's often resumed after the end of output. Whether the pump had to request the close is the mechanism itself. It still depends on scheduling at the margin: under that load the drain's close, which stays as the bound, won the race with a released host's exit in 1 of 25 in-box sessions. So the test requires some session to end on the pipe break, which a host that was not released never does.
- Inherit-cursor was first deferred as a fix for a ConPTY cursor bug that nobody had reported. Its real use is a frontend that already shows content when the child starts: VS Code sets it whenever a terminal has `initialText`, and a console host keeps the user's screen with it (verified in a VT terminal: without it the prompt and earlier lines were erased; with it they stayed and the child's output followed).
- Foreground process lookup belongs behind the existing Unix native boundary: `tcgetpgrp` supplies the foreground process group without spawning `ps`, preserving NativeAOT and avoiding a helper process on each editor poll. A process-group id is not always a live process id: after a pipeline leader exits, lookup must fall back to a remaining group member rather than reporting no active process.
- Output must be read on a thread the library owns. The former producer started on the caller's captured context (through `Task.Yield`) and then blocked inside `ReadFile` / `read(2)`, which deadlocked a UI thread before the first chunk and froze it on every idle read; every idle session also parked a thread-pool worker. A per-session reader thread that completed allocation-free waits, whose continuations run asynchronously, removed all three. The engines that later replaced it, one loop for every session on each OS, keep that and hold no thread per session.
- A batch file's arguments are parsed by `cmd.exe`, not by the MSVCRT rules, so quoting that programs read back correctly was an injection for `.bat` and `.cmd`. Two details only show up when trying. An injected `echo` can print its text with a stray quote after it (`INJECTED"`), so a test that looks for the exact line misses a working injection. Detecting the batch file by the name as given misses `script.cmd.` and `script.cmd `, which Windows opens as `script.cmd`. Trimming them is not enough either. `CreateProcess` also started `cmd.exe` for `script.cmd\.`, `script.cmd\sub\..`, `script.cmd\. `, and `script.cmd\sub\.. `, and with the first three an injected command in an argument ran, although `cmd.exe` could not find the script. `GetFullPathNameW` turns the last two into names that end with a backslash, so it does not predict this. Detection therefore resolves the dot segments itself and leaves a name that no file matches to fail in the lookup.
- Starting `cmd.exe` directly moves the script lookup into MiniPty, and it has to be the lookup `CreateProcess` makes. When `CreateProcess` started the batch file, its own search only decided whether the start failed. `cmd.exe` then looked the name up again from the child's working directory and `PATH`, so a script other than the one found could run. Probes with programs showed rules the documentation does not state. A name with a directory part is searched for like a bare name, the host executable's directory first. `PATH` entries are taken as written, without trimming or unquoting, and an empty entry after the last semicolon is not the current directory. A directory found first fails the start with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` rather than being skipped. A missing rooted script must fail in MiniPty, because `cmd.exe` would report it only in its output and with exit code 1. The same holds after the lookup: `CreateProcess` failed with `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` for an empty script, with `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` while another handle held it for writing or denied reading, and with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` for a link whose target is gone, where `cmd.exe` would have started and exited 1 or 0.
- Quoting by `char.IsWhiteSpace` misses spaces that `cmd.exe` splits a script's parameters on: U+180E is not white space to .NET, yet `cmd.exe` split on it as on U+3000, U+00A0, and U+2003. Quoting everything outside a short ASCII allow list covers them without listing them.
- The escaped length must not wrap. Each `%` takes 8 characters, and an `int` sum checked once after all arguments wrapped to 1,577 for 512 references to one string of 2^20 `%` characters, which passed the 8191 check. The length is now a `long` checked after each argument, so the sum stops at the first argument that crosses the limit.
- Never blocking is not enough for a UI consumer; it must also give the thread back. A read that completes synchronously never returns to the dispatcher, so a handler slower than the child's output found the next chunk buffered every time and kept the UI thread for the whole flood: with 2 ms of work per chunk, a callback posted to the UI context waited over a second. A yield must also be completed only after the awaiter has registered: a value task that is already complete when it is awaited runs the continuation inline, so the reader completes the yield from `OnCompleted`, which makes the core post it to the captured context. The budget is timed per thread, not per consumer, because a dispatcher starves per thread and several tabs share one UI thread; a per-consumer timestamp also cost every session 8 bytes. A consumer that awaits something else between reads can have its reads more than a budget apart, and each such read then yields once. That costs what a read that had to wait costs, and was accepted rather than tracking the dispatcher.
- A thread per session costs more than its start. A bare thread start allocates 137 bytes, and one pooled-array return on a fresh thread raised that to about 4.9 KB: the array pool allocates a per-thread cache on the first return, and the returned array is stranded in that cache when the thread exits. One-shot completion then grew its result buffers on the reader thread, so a new thread per session would have paid this on every spawn. The reader threads were therefore pooled across sessions, a parked thread serving the next session and exiting after 30 seconds idle, until the engines removed the thread per session altogether. The Windows output drivers are pooled the same way, for their 208-byte `PreAllocatedOverlapped`.
- One-shot completion writes into a sink where output is read instead of draining the buffer from a consumer task. With a bounded buffer, a consumer that only started draining after exit would block a bulk-output child before it could exit. Writing there needs no consumer thread and removed the pump task, the polling drain, and the timeout tasks: about 0.7 KB less per `CompleteAsync`.
- Coalescing needs a bound per chunk, not only a window per read. Each Unix continuation read of the reader threads waited its own 1 ms window, so a child writing small pieces faster than that (a progress meter, token streaming) had its output held until a 4 KiB slot filled: up to about 150 ms on macOS at one write every 0.5 ms. A budget of 2 ms from a slot's first read bounded it. The bridges' coalescing keeps the rule: every wait in a burst has a deadline, so no stream holds a chunk past about 2 ms.
- Measure a sub-millisecond window with `Stopwatch`, never with `Environment.TickCount64`. The ConPTY window was "1 ms" by `TickCount64`, which on Windows lasts until the next clock tick, up to about 16 ms. While a child wrote small pieces, the reader spun in its `Thread.Sleep(0)` loop for most of every tick: about 80% of a core for 20-byte writes every 1–10 ms. ConPTY's bulk slices arrive 20–45 µs apart, so a 500 µs `Stopwatch` window kept 32 KiB in 13 full chunks (12–13 before) and cut that reader load to about 10% at 5–10 ms intervals (about 40% at 1 ms). Trickle latency fell from p50 8 ms / max about 30 ms to p50 0.6 ms / max about 13 ms; the rest is ConPTY's own rendering, which delivers some writes up to about 15 ms late even with coalescing disabled.
- A .NET timer is no millisecond clock, on Windows or on Linux. A 1 ms `Timer` fired every 15.6 ms on Windows, the system timer's resolution, so the bridges' coalescing deadlines it served held a burst's tail for about 15 ms where macOS held it for about 1.3 ms. On Linux, timers take their due times from `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE`, which advances at the kernel's tick rate, and the same timer fired every 4 ms under a 250 Hz kernel (WSL2), while `Thread.Sleep(1)` and a 1 ms epoll wait each took 1.05 ms. A wait that must last about a millisecond needs a high-resolution waitable timer on Windows, rather than `timeBeginPeriod`, which raises the resolution for the whole process, and a wait timeout on the precise clock on Unix, which the I/O loop's own wait already is.
- Coalescing belonged to the reader, so every consumer got it. Capture used to record one chunk per transport read; slots that keep appending within the micro-window cut a 32 KiB capture's chunks and the metadata they cost (about 5 KB less on Windows). The Windows driver publishes each read as it completes, which a ring consumer batches by its own pace, but a sink is written once per read: a 32 KiB capture allocated 4.7 KB more again (9.3 KB with text). Capture now joins reads that follow one another within the windows the reader threads had used into one chunk itself, deciding per write from the reads' timestamps, and is back at 39.77 KB.
- A Unix master cannot be closed under its users: `close(2)` does not interrupt a `read` or `poll` blocked on the descriptor in another thread, and the number can be reused while that thread still uses it. The master is reference-counted, so it closes only after its users release it: the reader threads then, the loop's registration now, and input writes, resize, and EOT writes. A reader thread also needed a wake descriptor beside the master so that it could be stopped at all; the loop, which never blocks in a read, does not. This also resolved the resize race in which a concurrent drain closed the master during the `ioctl`.
- Let go of pooled resources before publishing completion. The reader first signaled end of output and only then dropped its reference to the buffer, so a consumer that disposed at once sometimes left the final release to the reader thread. The array then went back to the pool from that thread and stayed in its per-thread cache, and the next session's rent allocated a fresh 16 KiB array: the streaming benchmark intermittently averaged 7.2 KB instead of 1.7 KB. Releasing the buffer and parking the reader thread before completion became observable made both deterministic. One-shot sinks had the same problem: detaching their grown result buffers on the thread that resumed the caller left them in a worker's cache, and the next run's growth on the reader thread allocated again (intermittent 7 KB and 119 KB averages on the one-shot benchmarks). Finishing the result on the reader thread fixed that only while one thread fed and finished every sink; see the next lesson.
- A one-shot sink must cost the same on whichever thread feeds it, because output will be delivered by I/O completions on pool workers or by a loop shared by every session. Sinks that grew their results from the shared array pool, kept on one thread so that rents and returns met in one cache, allocated 6.4 KB per run beyond the result for bytes, and 81 KB with decoding, once the writes, the finish, and the result each ran on a thread that then ended. Growing by copying would also stall a shared loop for a time proportional to the output so far. Sinks now collect bytes and text in 16 KiB segments from a process-wide free list without per-thread caches (64 kept per element type, so one large capture cannot hold its memory for the rest of the process), decode straight into them, and merge them into the result arrays only on the caller's thread. The same runs now cost about 1.6 KB: the threads and the sink's own objects. The bookkeeping is paid on every run too. A first version kept the segments in a buffer object with four inline slots, twice the size of the growing array it replaced, while Capture had kept its bytes in a struct inside the sink, and text past 32 K characters needed an overflow array: 30–210 bytes more per one-shot benchmark run. The buffer is now a struct of a pooled segment table and a length, held in the sink.
- A sink's write is not one read. Since consumers take the contiguous backlog, a sink attached after several reads gets them as one write of up to the ring's 16 KiB. The decode scratch was still sized for one 4 KiB read, so `CompleteAsync` and Capture with `DecodeOutput` threw for such a backlog, and so did on-demand Capture text chunks for a chunk larger than one read. A test that wrote 4097 bytes passed anyway, because the pool had rounded the scratch up; 16 KiB of ASCII failed. Every sink test had fed one read at a time. Decoding now converts as much as fits and goes on, so a write of any length decodes, and the tests feed writes longer than a read and backlogs of several reads.
- An idle Windows session can wait without a buffer. A zero-byte overlapped read on MiniPty's end of the output pipe stays pending until output arrives, then completes with 0 bytes and leaves the output in the pipe; it completes at once when output is already waiting, and fails with `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE` once ConPTY's end closes. The session takes a ring only then, and the driver waits with a zero-byte read again after each read; the ring goes back to the pool once the consumer has released the last byte. An earlier driver posted the next read into the ring while the consumer had not caught up, to save that round trip, and canceled it with `CancelIoEx` once the consumer had. A consumer that keeps up catches up after every ConPTY write, so each write cost a canceled read: on the out-of-band ConPTY, which writes a flood about 256 B at a time, 12,000 thread-pool work items and 219–234 ms of CPU per MiB, against 8,200 and 156–172 ms with the zero-byte wait alone. Of the per-session costs, the completion-port binding (40 B) stays; the `PreAllocatedOverlapped` (208 B) is pooled with the driver object across sessions. `ThreadPool.BindHandle` with a reused `Overlapped` allocated nothing at all, but it throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` when the host runs on the Windows thread pool (`System.Threading.ThreadPool.UseWindowsThreadPool`), where `ThreadPoolBoundHandle` works (72 B there).
- A driver that reads on completions must give its thread back. A step that kept finding output never posted a read, so it kept its pool thread and its pin on the pipe for as long as the child wrote. After disposal that became a livelock: the step discarded output as fast as the flood refilled the pipe, disposal could not close the pipe that would end the flood, and `DisposeAsync` never completed, in about one of a thousand disposals during a flood (the step looped 350,000 times in 200 ms). A step now stops after 16 reads that complete at once and has the loop come back to it after the other sessions; on the runtime's completion port it went back to the pool and continued as a new work item. The plain flood test passed with the bug in place; a pipe with a large buffer filled before disposal reproduced it in two of three runs.
- On the runtime's completion port, a completion could arrive before the step that posted its read had recorded that the read was posted, and once it had, the completion might already be running the next step. That driver handed the completion's result to the step still running, and the posting step did everything it needed before it recorded the posted state. An early version asked for the consumer's "ring empty" wake after recording the state, where its cancel could reach the next step's read (found in review). The loop now runs every step and every completion on one thread, so a completion never runs beside its step. A step that resumed from a full ring also has to end the free-space handshake itself, or the post-exit drain never sees the transport go quiet: a test whose pipe stayed open after the child's exit never reached end of output.
- A Windows step that fails with a read posted must not end output at once. The read points into the driver, which goes back to the pool when output ends: the next session got the driver with the old read still posted, and when the failed session's pipe closed, that read's completion ended the next session's output. A step now records that a read is posted before anything that can fail. A failure with a read posted cancels the read, and the step that handles its completion ends output.
