Two tests fail a session through hooks, as a Unix test long had: once in a read, and once right after a zero-byte read is posted. The second reproduced the stale completion when the wait was removed.
- A loop must not wait again at once after a wait that failed. The Windows loop took a failed `GetQueuedCompletionStatus` with no completion, which only a port closed or broken under it returns, for a wake, and a test that fails every wait counted 18 million passes in 500 ms. It now backs off for 10 ms, as the Unix loop does after a failed `epoll_wait` or `kevent`. A pass counter lets the tests show that idle sessions, parked sessions, and a failed port do not spin the loop.
- On Linux the exit watcher's thread can be the I/O loop of every session, because it already waited on an epoll of the children's pidfds. Each master joins it, level-triggered, with the interest its state needs. A master whose slaves have all closed reports hang-up whatever the interest, so a session parked on a full ring, with no interest at all, made the loop spin: 750,000 passes in 500 ms while the consumer stayed away. Interest 0 now arms the registration for a single report (`EPOLLONESHOT`), and setting interest again re-arms it, which reports the hang-up then. 1,000 idle sessions went from 1,051 threads and 8.4 GB of reserved stacks to 31–50 threads and 240–396 MB (the rest are the pool workers a burst of connections injects), and with the coalescing window kept at first, echo latency stayed the same.
- A registration needs the descriptor to outlive it. epoll keeps a registration until every duplicate of the open file description closes, and a child the host forks on another thread holds duplicates until it execs, so a closed master's number could come back to the loop on a new descriptor. The loop therefore holds its own reference on the master from registration until it removes it, and every close asks the loop to remove it; only then can the last release close the descriptor.
- Disposal must still finish the pump at once on the loop, as it did on the reader thread: `DisposeAsync` waits for the pump, and a hung-up child may take its whole one-second grace. The loop finishes the pump and keeps the master registered to discard the child's output until the master closes, which replaced the watcher's separate discard path for these sessions.
- A bound per pass is cheap insurance, not something a test could show. The loop reads each session at most four times per pass, but a flood never starved another session's echo even with the bound removed, because a terminal delivers output more slowly than the loop reads it, so the flood's master runs dry between reads. The test that would have shown it passed either way, also with the flood going to a one-shot result, whose ring never fills.
- Session disposal takes two steps, and the loop can run between them. The pump is marked disposed first, so a read in flight discards, and only then does the backend hang the child up and decide who discards its output while the master stays open. A loop that served the session in between saw a disposed pump on a backend that was not yet disposed, ended the session, and removed its master, and the hang-up then left the child's output to nobody: the child blocked on a full terminal until the grace kill. It failed one of seven full Linux runs, and a test that marks the pump and lets the loop see it before disposing fails every time with the original code. The loop now goes on discarding whenever the pump is disposed, and the hang-up asks whether the loop still has the master registered rather than whether it ever had; either alone fixes it.
- One batching policy for both engines: publish each read as it completes. On Linux the 1 ms window cost a keystroke echo about 1 ms (p50 1.47 ms with it, 0.42 ms without), and dropping it took a flood through the WebSocket bridge from 7.7 to 15–17 frames per 32 KiB, about twice the Phase 0 baseline, which was accepted. A consumer still busy with its previous chunk takes what arrived meanwhile as one chunk, and Capture joins close reads in its sink.
- Post-exit quiet means the driver could read and found nothing. Time parked on a full ring had counted as silence, so a drain tick right after a stalled reader resumed could close a Unix master that still held output; resuming now restarts the quiet interval. A drain tick also needs the exit time: exit waits complete before the exit listener records it, so a completion could schedule ticks that read every deadline as long past. Ticks now wait for the exit to be recorded. Both came from review, not from failing tests.
- Check ring capacity on its own, never as the alternative branch to "a sink is attached". A failed completion can detach its sink between that check and the drain, and the reader then read into a full ring, overwriting an unread slot.
- A full ring after the close is not end of output. The pump used to finish when the post-exit close found the ring full, with whatever the transport still held (on Windows, ConPTY's frames flushed by the close) unread. Loaded CI runners, where the consumer released slots late, delivered 1–7 of 8 flushed bytes. The driver now parks on a full ring after the close as before it, and reads on once a slot is free.
- Scripted transports paced by sleeps need an order of magnitude of margin over the period they test. Reads every 50 ms against a 100 ms quiet period passed on desktops and failed on every hosted macOS run, where a sleeping scripted reader was scheduled 100–200 ms late; the scripted backends now report a 500 ms quiet period through `IPtyBackend.PostExitQuietMs` while the platform backends keep 100 ms.
- Stream's async-over-sync defaults are a trap for a stream over a blocking transport. `Input.WriteAsync` and the bytes overload of `WriteInputAsync` ran the write on a thread-pool worker and allocated 112–248 bytes per call. The input stream now overrides every asynchronous overload, and a write the terminal takes at once completes synchronously, allocation-free after the session's first write.
- On Unix the session's output driver writes the input a full tty input queue cannot take yet: it already waits on the master, so write readiness joins the same wait (the loop's registration of the master, whose write interest is set only while input is queued). The master is non-blocking, so callers never block, and `Dispose` fails queued writes itself rather than waiting on a writer. EOF is ordered input too: staged EOT waits until nothing is queued, or it would overtake input the child has not read.
- ConPTY takes input into its own buffer whether or not the child reads, but only while it can write its output. With a child writing output that nobody reads, ConPTY stops reading input after about 4 KiB, and a synchronous write blocked its caller; on a UI thread that also runs the output loop, that is a deadlock. MiniPty's end of the Windows input pipe is therefore overlapped. A write the pipe takes at once still completes synchronously, and allocates nothing after the first write creates the overlapped state. The rest is written by I/O completions, so no thread waits. The input benchmarks were measured with a child that reads, so they could not show this.
- Tests without a `SynchronizationContext` cannot see caller-context blocking: test runners resume continuations on the thread pool, where `Task.Yield` happens to leave the caller's thread. `PtyCallerContextTests` drives the API from a single-threaded context, and one posted probe is not enough there. The former Unix exit wait blocked for 100 ms and then yielded, so a probe slipped through between slices while the thread was blocked almost all the time. The tests therefore also measure how long the UI thread spends inside callbacks over a 500 ms idle window (well under 1 ms when it is free), timestamp their probes on the UI thread rather than through the pool, and count occupied pool workers (`GetMaxThreads` minus `GetAvailableThreads`) instead of timing a burst.
- Pool starvation starts at the minimum worker count, which is the processor count, not at some large number of sessions. With two parked workers per idle session, 16 sessions on 32 logical CPUs took a burst of 64 short work items from 60 ms to about 2 s, and on an 8-core laptop four tabs were enough.
- An isolated output chunk costs what the .NET thread pool charges for one continuation, plus one wake-up of the output driver. Measured per thread on Linux (WSL2) for 20 bytes every 10 ms read through `ReadOutputAsync`: the I/O loop woke once per chunk for 39–40 µs of CPU, and two pool workers woke once each for about 100 µs together, 151–185 µs in all. Without MiniPty, a thread that sleeps and completes one awaited `IValueTaskSource` per tick cost the same: 29–42 µs for that thread and two worker wake-ups, because the pool wakes a second worker whenever it takes an item, so that more work could run in parallel. The loop is at the floor of any reader that waits for output, and the rest is the price of an asynchronous consumer on the pool, which a consumer avoids only by batching. The first measurement, 165 µs, also carried the JIT's tiered recompilation in the process's first seconds (136–142 µs per chunk in that window).
- Every field on a per-session object is paid by every session. A one-byte field grew every session by 8 bytes once the backend's small fields filled their slot, and the Windows input queue and overlapped state cost every session 20–30 bytes as backend fields, including sessions that never write. State a session may never use lives in an object created on first use, per-thread state in a thread-static, and the out-of-band ConPTY in a subclass of the pseudo-console handle, so a session without it pays nothing. Widening a field counts too: the bridges' coalescing wait first stored its minimum in an `int` where the pump had a `bool`, and every session's pump grew from 184 to 192 B; a `short` kept the size, and the coalescing state lives in a subclass of the reader that only a bridge's session gets.
- Allocation-free exit observation needs care at every layer: the task is created only when someone awaits it, internal waits use a slot rather than a task, a method with a single await avoids an async state machine, and no exception is constructed that is not thrown (`Dispose` once built an `ObjectDisposedException` on every call). Pooled `ValueTask` builders did not help, because boxes returned on another thread were often not reused. A caught exception is an allocation too: the reader once ended output on a closed Windows handle by catching the marshaller's `ObjectDisposedException`, 330 bytes per out-of-band session, and now checks the handle first. A check before each call was not enough for the reader threads' Windows continuation reads, which made three marshalled calls per attempt for up to 500 µs: once the in-box host was released and wrote its last frame as the child exited, a session disposed right after exit threw in 24–47% of sessions (`Session_Exit0_WaitForExit` grew from 1.24 KB to 1.37–1.42 KB). They then pinned the handle once per window, called with the raw handle, and stopped when `IsClosed` turned true, which happens at once while the close waits for the pin; the completion driver pins the pipe once per step the same way.
- A reused `IValueTaskSource` needs both parties to let go. Resetting a queued-write entry as soon as its waiter had read the result raced the completer, which could still be signaling that waiter. An entry returns to the process-wide spare only after the completion has returned and the waiter has read the result.
- Writes that share a token are canceled newest first, because cancellation callbacks run in reverse registration order, so removing each from the head of the queue walked the whole queue per write: canceling 20,000 queued writes took 1,441 ms on macOS and 319–337 ms on Windows. Queued writes are doubly linked, and the same cancellation now takes 14 ms and 2–10 ms.
- A timeout that fires once needs a re-check after the wait is armed. The drain close timeout could land between a completion sink's state check and its arming the wait, which left no wait to signal: `CompleteAsync` would have hung instead of throwing. The sink re-checks after arming, with full fences on both sides. Review found this, not a failing test.
- Stamp quiet detection per read, not per slot. Stamping a slot's last read after its coalescing micro-window let the window's empty tail postpone the post-exit close by up to a clock tick, which made capture runs about 10 ms slower.
- A job object's guarantees rest on details of its handle. The job list is an attribute value, which must outlive the attribute list and not only `CreateProcess`: the session keeps its list until disposal, so the handle array lives in the same allocation. The host-crash guarantee holds only while the session's handle is the job's only one, so the child is created without handle inheritance and the handle is never duplicated. And with a job, `Kill` cannot stop at the child's exit, or `Kill` and `Dispose` would end different sets of processes.
- A data signal may claim only a wait that its output is still there for, and only the wait it read. The pump counts output and then signals, so a consumer that was not waiting can take that output in between, finish with it, and arm a new wait; claiming that wait completed it with nothing to read, and the enumeration failed with "signaled without a state change". A consumer that withdraws a wait because it saw the output itself can likewise arm another before a delayed claim lands. Through the WebSocket bridge the failure ended the session and lost the rest of a 32 MiB flood, once in about ten runs on Linux. Each armed wait now carries a generation, and a data signal claims it only while output is unread, checked after reading the wait. A stress test with consumers that do nothing reproduced the failure within two seconds in every run before the fix. The generation alone did not fix it: the instrumented failure showed the claim taking a wait armed after the output was consumed, which is a new wait and not a stale one.
- A chunk is all contiguous unread output, not one read. With four fixed slots, a consumer that fell behind still took one read at a time, so the WebSocket bridge sent a frame per read even when several were waiting: 8.0 frames per 32 KiB of flood. A byte ring hands a slow consumer every contiguous read at once, which cut that to 5.2–5.7 on Windows and 7.7–7.8 on Linux at the same throughput. The ring holds bytes, so it also stopped filling up with a few small ConPTY frames. Its buffer comes from a free list without thread affinity rather than the shared array pool, because the party that releases a ring last varies by thread.
- A string that names a program has to be checked for NUL. The batch-file path rejected NUL, and so did the environment, but a program's `FileName`, its arguments, and `WorkingDirectory` passed it through. The operating system then read only the part before it. On Windows `"...\cmd.exe\0C:\allowed\safe.exe"` started `cmd.exe` and dropped every argument after it; on Linux `"/bin/sh\0/usr/bin/safe"` started `/bin/sh`. `Path.GetFileName` read the allowed name in both cases, so a host that allowed programs by name would have started another one. A path of 260 characters or more already failed in `Path.GetFullPath`, so the same mistake behaved differently by length. `Pty.Start` now rejects a NUL in all four on every platform. A security review of the long-path change found this, not a failing test.
- A probe of the `\\?\` prefix concluded that `CreateProcess` refuses it as an application name (error 3). The probe's path had been built from a forward-slash path (`C:/Users/...`), which a `\\?\` path takes literally. With backslashes the prefixed path starts. A probe of path handling builds its paths with the separators the code under test will see.
- A rollback switch has to keep the old code whole, not only choose a driver. The `AppContext` switch back to reader threads that shipped with the engines during the transition could not just pick the reader: a blocking read is not allowed on a handle opened for overlapped I/O, so on Windows it also brought back the anonymous output pipe, the synchronous cancel of a blocked read, and the `PIPE_NOWAIT` window, and on Unix the wake descriptors and their wait. It was removed with the threads before any release. Tests that script a transport with blocking code keep a small driver of their own, with a thread per session, that follows the pump's producer contract as the platform drivers do. A Unix master the loop cannot register no longer falls back to a thread either: the start fails, which a test hook that refuses one session's registration covers.
